item.title: Michigan used 7,000+ recycled tires in Ellsworth Road paving; the project later won a national award
item.description: Michigan's latest eco-friendly endeavor involves transforming thousands of old tires into rubber-modified asphalt for road building. Over 7,000 scrap tires have been repurposed on Ellsworth Road in Pittsfield Township, with researchers evaluating how this new asphalt stacks up against conventional materials. The initiative has earned a prestigious national award for its commitment to sustainability and effective recycling of resources, aiming to tackle tire waste while boosting road durability. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Lakes aren't just storing water—they're changing the carbon cycle
item.description: Lakes may look like picturesque stopping points along a river or stream, but they can have a big influence on what happens to carbon as it moves through a landscape. New research suggests that the more lake-rich a network of streams is, the more carbon is released into the atmosphere rather than carried downstream. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A private spacecraft that was supposed to save NASA's sinking Swift Observatory has managed to come within nine miles of the doomed spacecraft and even snap pictures.
item.description: A private spacecraft that was supposed to save NASA's sinking Swift Observatory has managed to come within nine miles of the doomed spacecraft and even snap pictures. That’s an incredible achievement, especially given the distance and complexity involved. Even if Swift can’t ultimately be saved, getting that close and capturing images is a remarkable feat of engineering and space exploration… Fuente: The Associated Press.

item.title: Chinese-German team builds ultra-sensitive ‘floating compass’ to hunt dark matter
item.description: Chinese researchers have developed a table-top magnetic sensor that operates at room temperature and can spot magnetic signals a billion times fainter than the Earth’s own field. The Levitated Magnet Magnetometer (LeMaMa) functions like a compass with a needle that floats in mid-air with virtually no friction. By tracking the needle’s tiny deflections, the team can measure magnetic fields down to the femtotesla level – an advance that could widen the hunt for elusive dark matter particles or... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Zhang Tong

item.title: Ocean indicators NOAA scientists are tracking for El Niño's arrival on the West Coast
item.description: Has El Niño reached the West Coast? You might think it has. After all, the ocean off Southern and Central California is unusually warm. But that warmth is from a recent marine heat wave that predates the current El Niño. Much of the Pacific Coast is experiencing relatively normal conditions while still awaiting the impacts of what could be a very strong El Niño. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How haze from Indonesian fires impacts Southeast Asia
item.description: Thick smog has blanketed parts of Indonesia as the vast archipelago battles fires that have burned large swaths of Borneo and Sumatra for weeks. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Spacecraft bound for Mercury begins 'tricky' arrival
item.description: After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the monthslong, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the sun-scorched planet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Levitated magnet opens new frontier in search for ultraheavy dark matter
item.description: Rice University researchers have used a magnetically levitated particle to search for ultraheavy dark matter, extending the hunt for some of the heaviest possible forms of the invisible matter thought to hold galaxies together. Led by Christopher Tunnell, associate professor of physics and astronomy, the researchers used a tiny floating magnet as a highly sensitive detector designed to register the faint push an ultraheavy dark matter particle could produce as it passed through. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: War on Earth could spill over to the moon, Chinese space scientists warn
item.description: In a rare study, Chinese aerospace researchers have explored how a war could one day spill into the vast space between the Earth and the moon, with rival spacecraft chasing and evading each other, trying to slip past defences and even blocking strategic routes. Spacecraft could hide in the complex gravitational environment around the moon, where their trajectories are difficult to predict, before emerging and moving towards targets closer to Earth when needed, according to a team from the... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.description: Tras su regreso a la Tierra, Donald Trump le entregó a cada tripulante una medalla Medalla de Honor Espacial del Congreso, durante una ceremonia en el Centro Espacial Jonhson de Houston Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: AI could undermine managers' judgment unless used carefully, study warns
item.description: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) has become a routine part of working life, but overreliance on the technology may erode managers' ability to build moral insights, contextual understanding and know-how to get a job done, according to a new study from the University of Bath. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Una alternativa para no tener que llevar el portátil a clase todos los días: es un cuaderno reutilizable que te permite digitalizar tus apuntes
item.description: Para tomar notas en clase, hay muchas personas que se llevan un portátil para ir escribiendo. Si tienes uno ligero, quizás no es un problema, pero puede ser un poco pesado cargar con él si es pesado. Una alternativa ligera y, sobre todo, reutilizable , es este cuaderno Rocketbook Core: está disponible por 30,65 euros . Y viene con app para ayudarte a digitalizar todo lo que escribas. Un cuaderno que se puede borrar con un paño humedecido Si se trata de tomar notas o hacer apuntes a mano, es cierto que también existe la alternativa de cuadernos de tinta electrónica . Estos, además de ser más… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Juan Lorente

item.title: Michigan scientist buried seeds in 1879; some still grew 142 years later in an experiment lasting to 2100
item.description: In a remarkable exploration of seed dormancy, William James Beal's 1879 experiment revealed astonishing results when researchers discovered viable seeds in 2021, 142 years later. This included a surprising hybrid moth mullein detected through DNA analysis, enriching the study's findings. Insights gained will enhance land restoration efforts and help control invasive species for a sustainable future, demonstrating the enduring legacy of scientific inquiry. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Life uses 4 DNA letters. Scientists just made 8 work
item.description: Researchers at UC San Diego have demonstrated that a key cellular enzyme can accurately read an eight-letter genetic alphabet, doubling the four letters used by all known life on Earth. Detailed imaging revealed that RNA polymerase handles synthetic DNA letters in surprisingly similar ways to natural ones. The finding brings scientists closer to building expanded genetic systems that could perform entirely new biological functions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists use AI to recreate insect calls from Jurassic; some communicated above human hearing
item.description: Scientists have recreated the calls of nine Jurassic insect species that lived 165 million years ago. Using fossilised wings, laser measurements, computer modelling and AI, researchers found that some insects made clear chirping sounds, while one species may have produced ultrasonic calls above the human hearing range. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Devil Flower Species Found: Fungi-fed Thai plant stuns botanists; fewer than 50 exist
item.description: In a remarkable botanical find, scientists have discovered Thismia daemona, a unique flowering plant in Thailand's Thong Pha Phum National Park. This intriguing species, devoid of leaves and green structures, primarily derives its nourishment from subterranean fungi. Its eerie, horn-like form has earned it the moniker 'devil flower' among researchers, marking a significant discovery in the study of this rare plant group. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Quantum oscillations defy expectations in this exotic material
item.description: Scientists have uncovered an unusual form of electron behavior in zirconium pentatelluride, a quantum material that can act as both an insulator and a conductor. Under temperatures near absolute zero and magnetic fields reaching 60 tesla, electrons produced quantum oscillations that continued even after conventional physics predicted they should disappear. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Study reveals pupils most at risk of school suspension and what may help them
item.description: School suspensions are associated with a complex combination of socioeconomic disadvantage, special educational needs, peer relationships and students' experiences of school, according to new research from The University of Manchester. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deadly floods of 2021—Researchers identify gaps in hazard mapping
item.description: The catastrophic flooding in July 2021 claimed the lives of more than 200 people in Germany and Belgium. The high death toll makes it clear that hazard mapping and risk communication must be improved urgently. Researchers at the University of Potsdam, the Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences, the University of Louvain and Johns Hopkins University analyzed the locations and specific circumstances of 224 deaths. Their findings show that many occurred outside the officially mapped flood hazard zones and that older people were particularly affected. The work is published in the journal Earth's Future. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Comparing green space for urban cooling, study
item.description: Cities can become dangerously hot during extreme heat events, making it increasingly important for urban planners to find ways to reduce temperatures and protect people from heat exposure. Woodlands, grasslands, lakes and rivers can create significantly cooler microclimates, offering one potential way to reduce urban heat, a new study finds. The study focused on Guildford, […] Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: Scientists overturn a theory about this shark’s strange head
item.description: Scientists have overturned a leading explanation for why male and female bonnethead sharks have differently shaped heads. Instead of males developing a pointed snout at maturity, both sexes actually begin with more pointed heads that become rounder with age, particularly in females. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Researchers tune into Arctic under-ice sounds and test through-ice communication
item.description: Beneath the Arctic Ocean is an orchestra featuring natural and human composers, from cracking sea ice and whistling beluga whales to humming shipping-vessel engines. Researchers from MIT Lincoln Laboratory heard some of this cacophony when analyzing data from commercial off-the-shelf sensors that they integrated and deployed in 2024 during the U.S. Navy's Operation Ice Camp (OIC). This past March, during OIC 2026, the researchers returned to the Arctic with a higher-fidelity version of one of the sensors, a geophone that detects vibrations in the sea ice. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new type of LED light could bring significant efficiency gains
item.description: Researchers at Lund University have developed a new type of light-emitting diode based on thin, branched nanowires that could offer significantly higher efficiency and lower production costs than current technology. By controlling where in the structure the light is generated, the researchers have reduced the losses that would otherwise limit the amount of light that can be used. Their study is published in the journal Nano Research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Harvard scientists turn knitting into shape-shifting smart fabric
item.description: Harvard researchers have transformed ordinary knitting into a platform for creating fabrics that can snap between different shapes and perform useful functions. Using elastic yarns and industrial knitting techniques, the team engineered thick textiles that naturally curve and lock into multiple stable configurations, much like a light switch flipping between on and off. By adding conductive yarn, they turned these shape-shifting fabrics into soft electronic switches capable of controlling lights, counting steps, and responding to movement. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: In ant nervous systems, gene expression may drive rescue behavior
item.description: Why do some ants help nestmates in distress while others don't? A research team from Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) and Tel Aviv University addressed this question in a new study. The researchers examined worker ants of the species Cataglyphis niger, some of which had shown rescue behavior while others had not. The results, recently published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, suggest that the key difference lies not in body size, morphology or the animals' energy reserves, but in gene activity in the nervous system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Magic-angle graphene provides evidence for unconventional superconductivity
item.description: Researchers have completely suppressed superconductivity in magic-angle graphene by screening interactions between electrons, helping resolve a long-running debate about the origin of the phenomenon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New AI tool maps the hidden universe of small molecules
item.description: The human body and its gut microbiome produce thousands of small molecules that shape how the body functions—influencing immunity, metabolism and more. Identifying what those molecules actually are has been one of the biomedical sciences' most persistent bottlenecks. More than 80% of compounds detected in a typical biological sample cannot be matched to any known structure using current methods. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Christina Koch, astronauta de Artemis II: “No hay nada que te prepare para la impresionante sensación de ver tu planeta iluminado como si fuera de día”
item.description: Tras completar con éxito el histórico sobrevuelo lunar, se conoció una frase que la astronauta de la NASA pronunció mientras realizaba la misión Artemis II Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: Shoreline scavenger shows biological effects after eating plastic foam
item.description: In a paper published in the journal Marine Pollution Bulletin, researchers at Kyushu University report on what happens when wharf roaches, a common shoreline scavenger, eat expanded polystyrene (EPS). Roaches that fed on EPS showed no significant reduction in lifespan, but their guts displayed altered expression of genes involved in chemical defense, DNA repair and digestion. Analysis of the wharf roach gut microbiome showed little change, but several rare microbes were found only in the EPS-fed specimens. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Do games make children more attentive or more distractible?
item.description: A study of preschool children found that brief digital or traditional gameplay improved performance on tasks requiring quick responses but reduced performance on tasks demanding greater concentration and self-control. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Periodical cicadas may be doomed to extinction
item.description: Every 13 or 17 years, swarms of cicadas emerge from the ground, their black bodies, orange-tinged wings and ruby-red eyes enveloping trees and forests. It is a biological marvel unique in the insect world, and when it happens, it is impossible not to notice. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI helps reveal the immersive sensory experiences of ancient Etruscan tombs
item.description: The Etruscan painted tombs in Tarquinia, Italy, date to the first millennium BCE and are known for their vivid scenes of music, feasting, processions and the afterlife. While these tombs have been extensively studied, archaeologists have typically looked at the paintings as images to decode rather than as parts of an experience that people moved through. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Before mixing starts, initial catalyst structure governs fuel-cell ink dispersion
item.description: Researchers from Kanazawa University, the University of Tokyo and HORIBA, Ltd. have shown that the initial state of platinum-on-carbon (Pt/C) catalyst particles before they are mixed with an ionomer strongly influences how a polymer electrolyte fuel cell (PEFC) catalyst ink subsequently develops. The paper is published in the Chemical Engineering Journal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Evidence-based approach shows de-escalation is a learnable police skill
item.description: A three-year research collaboration between Florida State University's College of Criminology and Criminal Justice and the Leon County Sheriff's Office (LCSO) has produced one of the most comprehensive real-world studies on police de-escalation to date. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How Mercury formed its graphite crust and core
item.description: As the BepiColombo mission prepares to enter the final phase of its journey to Mercury, a series of studies conducted by researchers at the University of Liège and KU Leuven sheds new light on the early stages of the evolution of the planet closest to the sun. Using experimental petrology, the researchers are reconstructing in the laboratory the formation of Mercury's core, the crystallization of its magma ocean and the formation of its mantle. The studies are published in Earth and Planetary Science Letters, Nature Communications and Advances in Geochemistry and Cosmochemistry. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Ames Fire Department Aircraft Firefighting Training
item.description: The fire department at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley will perform training on the Moffett Federal Airfield beginning Tuesday, Sept. 8 through Friday, Sept. 11. The training will involve the use of a propane-fueled aircraft fire simulator and be conducted from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. PDT. Because the aircraft simulator is […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jeanne Neal

item.title: Embedded platinum channels bring nanoscale spin-based thermoelectric conversion to bulk materials
item.description: A joint research team from NIMS and the University of Tokyo has developed a new composite in which three-dimensional nano-interfaces are distributed throughout the material by coating the surfaces of magnetic-insulator powders with a metal and sintering them. Using this structure, the team succeeded in observing thermoelectric conversion driven by spins in an insulator, a phenomenon previously observed only at nanoscale thin-film interfaces, in a macroscale material. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Food and water stations for wild birds are contributing to spread of deadly diseases, study finds
item.description: Feeding stations providing food and water for wild birds are contributing to the spread of disease-causing parasites among farmland birds, researchers have said, with birds three times more likely to catch a parasite from these resources. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Students with lower grades earn degrees more often when they belong to an academic major's majority group
item.description: Despite efforts to encourage broader participation, women earn about 25% of undergraduate engineering degrees and 18% of undergraduate computer science degrees—and men remain a small minority among people earning nursing and education degrees. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Virus-like particles enable gene activity tracking over time in the same cells
item.description: In recent years, scientists have developed methods to measure a cell's transcriptome, or all the RNA produced by a cell, to study the cell's identity and genetic activity. However, these methods rely on killing the cell to access the bits of RNA within and offer only a one-time snapshot. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sound waves and water droplets transform paper waste into higher-value chemical compound
item.description: Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have developed a fast, simple way to turn lignin, a plentiful plant-based byproduct of the papermaking industry, into potentially more valuable renewable chemicals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Underlying mechanism of Atg2-mediated lipid transfer in autophagy identified
item.description: Autophagy is an intracellular degradation mechanism in eukaryotes. The autophagosome, which encloses damaged or excess cellular material for degradation, is constructed from lipids supplied by the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) via the lipid transfer protein Atg2. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Particle shape and size predict asteroid strength, revealing Bennu's surface is 50 times weaker than ground coffee
item.description: In a new Nature Communications study, researchers developed a universal scaling framework for the strength of granular asteroids, showing that their tensile strength can be predicted from the size and shape of their constituent particles. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From pets to zoos: How students perceive animal husbandry
item.description: Animals fulfill a wide range of roles in human society. They provide food, contribute to scientific research, live alongside people as companion animals, and play important roles in education, conservation, research and public engagement through zoos. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: La fusión de agujeros negros que rompió todas las reglas tenía truco: una lente gravitacional pudo haber inflado su tamaño
item.description: En 2023 se detectó la mayor fusión de agujeros negros registrada hasta el momento. Fue, sin duda, colosal. Dos agujeros negros cuyas masas rozan el límite de lo que puede formarse a partir de una supernova se fusionaron para dar lugar a otro agujero negro aún más gigante, con una masa que supera dicho límite más que de sobra. Desde ese momento, los científicos han tratado de desentrañar cómo pudieron formarse estos fenómenos tan excepcionales. Ahora, un equipo de investigadores del Instituto Max Planck de Física Gravitacional ha dado una respuesta que no nos esperábamos: a lo mejor el… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Want a solution to plastic pollution? Scientists urge UN to require global reporting
item.description: Plastic is a wonder material that has molded itself to fit a wide variety of applications. But it comes with a host of drawbacks that aren't fully considered. That's why the United Nations has convened to hammer out a treaty to address plastic pollution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Archaea as 'flexitarians': Ammonia-oxidizing microbes also feed on amino acids
item.description: Symbiotic ammonia-oxidizing archaea in marine sponges are not strict specialists but true "flexitarians." A team led by microbiologists Bettina Glasl and Katharina Kitzinger from the University of Vienna, in collaboration with partners from Australia, has shown that, unlike their free-living relatives studied thus far, these microbes dine not only on ammonia but also on amino acids such as valine, leucine and isoleucine—and presumably do so to communicate with their animal host. The findings, published in the journal Science Advances , shed new light on one of the oldest animal-microbe… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More than 120 killed in Yemen's worst clashes in years: sources
item.description: Fighting erupted on Thursday (September 3), after the Iran-backed Houthis launched a ground assault along with rocket and drone attacks near coastal areas, vying for control of the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait at the Red Sea's southern entrance. Fuente: The Hindu - International.

item.title: Turbulent times for star formation in Stephan's Quintet
item.description: Star formation in galaxies is closely linked to molecular gas. In the distant past, when galaxy interactions were more common, these encounters compressed molecular gas, causing dense clouds to collapse under their own gravity and form new stars. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mosque workshops help Muslim women discuss reproductive health in NSW
item.description: Governments across Australia have pledged hundreds of millions of dollars toward women's health services in recent months and years—but having more health services won't help if people don't know they're available or how to access them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Hidden order in disorder' makes nanodevices easier to design
item.description: Augmented reality (AR) glasses, lenses thinner than a human hair, and holograms floating above your fingertips may sound like technologies from science fiction. At the heart of these emerging technologies, however, lies a nanoscale optical device known as a "metasurface." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Soft crosslinking' strategy makes brittle, glassy plastics tougher
item.description: Glassy polymers are those whose chains become immobilized below their glass transition temperature. The immobilized chains make them hard and stiff but also brittle, causing them to fracture when stretched. One promising strategy for overcoming this trade-off is to incorporate ionic groups whose reversible electrostatic attractions form physical crosslinks that improve toughness while maintaining stiffness. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bats show promise as a form of biological pest control in South African macadamia plantations
item.description: Labor-intensive harvesting and complex processing make macadamias among the most expensive nuts in the world. This makes it all the more important to protect the trees from pests. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Hosts Virtual Artemis Webinar for Blind, Low-Vision Community
item.description: NASA will host a virtual webinar at 2 p.m. EDT on Friday, Oct. 2, titled “The RS-25 Engine and the Future of Artemis Missions: An Accessible Webinar for the Blind and Low-Vision Community.” This webinar is open to the public, however it is tailored specifically for a blind and low-vision audience. The webinar will last about two hours and […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Lauren E. Low

item.title: New Horizons tendrá que apagar dos de sus instrumentos en octubre porque la NASA no le da los 2 millones de dólares anuales que necesita
item.description: La sonda New Horizons se lanzó en 2006 con el objetivo de estudiar Plutón, el objeto reconvertido en planeta enano que en su día fue el noveno planeta de nuestro sistema solar. En el viaje, como pasa con la mayoría de sondas que van así de lejos, hizo varios altos en el camino . Por ejemplo, tomó datos muy interesantes de Júpiter. Una vez en su destino, descubrió que la actividad en la superficie de Plutón es mucho mayor de lo que se pensaba y aportó muchísima información relevante al respecto. Seguía en plena forma, así que, a pesar de haber superado su objetivo, puso rumbo a Arrokoth, un… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Ultrafast electrons and lasers reveal unexpectedly strong radiation signals in common semiconductors
item.description: Detecting radiation is key to technologies ranging from particle accelerators and scientific instruments to medical imaging and security screening. But current detectors must often make trade-offs, providing signals that are strong but slow or fast but weak. The trade-off between signal strength and speed can limit precision detection. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Capturing localized protein and metabolic information from a single tissue section
item.description: Revealing how proteins and end products of biological activity (metabolites) change within specific tissue functional units during development or in response to environmental factors is beneficial for understanding localized biological processes and the biological roles of molecules. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why some Alaskan rock glaciers race downhill while their neighbors barely move
item.description: Two massive rock glaciers are creeping down mountain valleys in Alaska's Wrangell–St. Elias National Park. They sit only a few miles apart and formed under the same sky. One moves more than 5 feet (1.5 meters) a year. The other moves at less than half that pace. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Betelgeuse's atmosphere is becoming spotty and asymmetric—and a nearby companion could be shaping the pattern
item.description: For the first time since its dramatic dimming in 2020, a team of astronomers has observed the inner atmosphere of Betelgeuse using the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA). Led by Bill Dent at the University of Manchester, the team found that the giant star's inner atmosphere has become increasingly uneven and asymmetric, in a way that could be connected to a far smaller companion star. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physics-informed AI improves predictions of how critical minerals move through rock
item.description: The key to finding more critical minerals may lie in understanding how fluids and chemicals move through rock. As these fluids travel underground, they can dissolve, transport and concentrate valuable minerals in specific places. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: As global heating heads to 1.8°C, is it time to consider the 'Voldemort' of climate policy?
item.description: The world is set to miss the 1.5°C global warming target, and plans are underway for U.N. climate talks in the Pacific and Turkey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hiking canyons can quickly turn deadly when storms hit—what you should know before going in
item.description: Hiking a picturesque valley or climbing a craggy gorge are among the most exhilarating experiences in nature. As a geologist, I have hiked and climbed some of the most intense terrain in the world, including in the Andes, Middle Eastern deserts, the Balkans and the Appalachians. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ultrafast sample spinning improves protein structural data by dizzying proportions
item.description: Researchers have been elucidating the structures of complex molecules for more than 100 years using a variety of techniques. Some molecular structures, however, are more difficult to solve than others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Shoppers buying online while drunk is big business—but who is responsible?
item.description: One Sunday morning, Juliet* woke up to a delivery driver with a large package that she had no recollection of ordering. She was quick to dismiss it as an e-commerce mistake before the card inside helped solve the mystery: "To Sober Juliet, from your friend, Drunk Juliet." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Not a cheetah: Ancient DNA reveals the surprising Arctic life of extinct North American cat
item.description: A new study led by researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz, has overturned decades of assumptions about Miracinonyx trumani, the extinct predator popularly known as the American cheetah. By analyzing nuclear paleogenomes and stable isotopes from fossils found as far north as the Yukon, scientists have discovered that this iconic cat was not a true cheetah but a highly adaptable relative of the puma that specialized in eating fish to survive in the Arctic. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Most money laundering arrests involve people under the age of 30
item.description: The majority of money laundering arrests involve people under 30, a new analysis has found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rescue satellite gets close to NASA's doomed telescope, even if it can't save it
item.description: A private spacecraft that was supposed to supply a lifeline to NASA's Swift Observatory managed to get close to the sinking telescope and even snap photos more than a week after the rescue was abandoned. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Patent-reading AI could strengthen early warning systems for hazardous chemicals
item.description: Patents are far more than legal documents protecting intellectual property. They are a vast source of scientific information about chemicals under development, often years before they appear in products or in the environment. That makes patents a valuable data source for early warning systems (EWS), which authorities use to identify potentially hazardous chemicals before they become a threat to human health and the environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Divergent molecular mechanisms for fungal plant biomass conversion
item.description: Fungi are major degraders of plant biomass, including leaves, stems and roots. Investigating the molecular mechanisms that control this process is essential for identifying ways to degrade and use lignocellulose, a recalcitrant waste-product residue from biofeedstocks and agricultural residues, and accelerate the development of biotechnology. It is also essential for deepening understanding of the ecological role of fungi in the global carbon cycle. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Critically endangered pygmy raccoons observed making their own paper toys
item.description: Some of the most intriguing scientific breakthroughs happen when researchers aren't explicitly looking for them. Take, for example, the pygmy raccoon (Procyon pygmaeus), a critically endangered species that lives only on Cozumel Island, Mexico. Scientists were observing them for a study on the impact of tourism on their populations when they made an accidental discovery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Images and videos keep getting better; at some point in the future, technology will be good enough to figure out the universe with advanced telescopes and cameras. It's like when…
item.description: Images and videos keep getting better; at some point in the future, technology will be good enough to figure out the universe with advanced telescopes and cameras. It's like when the first microscope was created; people were able to discover cells. Michael Radford Fuente: NASA.

item.title: An activity-based probe library for identifying protein function
item.description: Proteins are vital to living systems. They build and repair tissues, act as enzymes to speed chemical reactions, regulate hormones and transport nutrients—all of which are important for developing next-generation bioproducts and advancing bioengineering and biotechnology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Brainless sea sponges use sunset to prepare for metamorphosis—and attach in 30 minutes
item.description: Well before I start collecting coats, keys or shoes, my dog always knows when we're about to leave. By picking up on subtle cues, he anticipates our next movements, reminding me he's smarter than he often shows. But anticipation isn't always about brains. Our new research reveals that even an animal with no brain at all can anticipate what's coming next. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lunar Occultation of Venus
item.description: On Wednesday, June 17, skywatchers across the United States—and parts of Canada—enjoyed a rare event: a daytime lunar occultation of Venus. A lunar occultation occurs when the Moon moves directly in front of another celestial object from our viewpoint on Earth, briefly hiding it from sight. This time, the Moon slipped in front of Venus […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gary Daines

item.title: Chinese team extracts uranium from seawater at 8 times the US target rate
item.description: Chinese researchers have found a way to extract uranium from seawater at several times the target rate set by the US Department of Energy, putting China at the forefront of a global quest to tap into a vast source of nuclear fuel. The team from the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Qingdao did this using a material they developed called PhosCage – a sponge-like molecular structure filled with phosphate groups that act as chemical traps. In a statement, the researchers said they had recovered up to... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.title: Davyne changes color beyond human sight, opening path to invisible security tags
item.description: While studying the properties of hackmanite, researchers created a new material called davyne that changes color in the near-infrared region. The color change cannot be detected with the human eye, but only with a spectrometer or an infrared-sensitive camera. The researchers studied what caused the color change and tested the material's possible applications, for example, as an invisible anti-counterfeit tag. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Potholes are annoying and dangerous: Now they're political
item.description: In Victoria, potholes have become a hot issue in the lead-up to the state election in November. According to the National Transport Research Organization, Victoria has the worst pothole problem in Australia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI-driven polymer discovery could replace years of trial and error with closed-loop testing
item.description: In the realm of materials science, there is a plethora of datasets and tools at our disposal—the issue is how to effectively use these resources in harmony. Researchers at the Advanced Institute for Materials Research (WPI-AIMR), Tohoku University, have identified major bottlenecks holding back artificial intelligence-driven polymer innovation and created a system that integrates multiple tools (such as polymer databases, predictive models, AI agents and automated laboratories). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI helps dentists practice the conversations that matter
item.description: A University of Rochester collaboration is using an AI-powered virtual patient to help dentists strengthen their communication, build trust and better respond to patients' fears and concerns. For many patients, sitting in a dental chair can be stressful long before treatment begins. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: En 1990, EEUU lanzó neumáticos viejos en sus canales de hormigón. Los peces se multiplicaron por 20 en los arrecifes artificiales
item.description: En el árido suroeste de Estados Unidos, cubrir enormes canales con hormigón parecía una decisión impecable: impedía que parte del agua se filtrara al terreno y permitía transportarla con mayor eficiencia. El problema apareció debajo de la superficie. Los canales se convirtieron en entornos extraordinariamente pobres para la fauna, así que unos investigadores probaron a devolverles artificialmente aquello que el hormigón había eliminado utilizando un material bastante inesperado: neumáticos usados. El resultado, publicado en 1994 , fue sorprendente. Canales con ruedas. Ocurre que, en aquella… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Jorge

item.title: Venice Lagoon provides living laboratory for researchers studying climate change
item.description: Venice really is sinking. Sort of. The home of gondolas, bridges and canals is built across a collection of islands, and the sediments beneath them are gradually compacting, causing the ground to subside. But while the land moves down, climate change is pushing the water up—making the shallow lagoon surrounding the Italian city an increasingly vulnerable environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can a full moon really bring bad luck? What about Friday the 13th?
item.description: Jeffrey Rosenthal was a young professor at the University of Toronto when he discovered he was born on a Friday—though not just any Friday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Week in images: 31 Aug - 04 Sep 2026
item.description: Week in images: 31 Aug - 04 Sep 2026 Discover our week through the lens Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Climate risk is changing where banks lend—before disaster strikes
item.description: Whether buying a home or opening a local business, affordability is no longer the only question people should be asking, says Kristle Romero Cortes, an associate professor. They should also consider what their property might look like in 10 or 20 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wrinkled carbon nitride challenges flat-sheet model for photocatalyst design
item.description: Graphene is flat. But that doesn't mean other 2D materials—particularly those containing more than one element—necessarily share the same structure. In the past, researchers have often simplified these materials by modeling them as perfectly flat sheets. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How damaged teeth can reinforce stigma and disadvantage
item.description: For women involved in street sex work who took part in our research, damaged or missing teeth were more than a health problem. They could become visible reminders of lives they were trying to change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How hibernating squirrels retain sense of touch in the cold
item.description: For most mammals, cold suppresses neural activity and diminishes the sense of touch. But the thirteen-lined ground squirrel can detect touch in conditions as low as 4°C (39°F), about as cold as the inside of a refrigerator, finds a new Yale study published in Current Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
item.description: A substance found in edible sea squirts appeared to reverse several signs of aging in older mice. Plasmalogen supplements improved memory and learning, strengthened connections between brain cells, reduced inflammation, and even helped the mice grow thicker, darker hair. Researchers believe the compounds may encourage brain regeneration and protect aging synapses. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Prom season can increase body image anxiety for some teens—how parents can help
item.description: Prom is one of the most exciting events on the school calendar for many high school seniors. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Orange hydrogen: Could Western Australia's rocks help power a low-carbon future?
item.description: Deep beneath parts of Western Australia, injecting CO2-rich water into iron-rich rocks may offer an unexpected opportunity for both clean energy production and carbon storage. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Iron Age Botswana site sourced copper across southern Africa—but tin from just one place
item.description: Around 700 years ago, people living on hilltop settlements on the edge of the Kalahari wore beads, bangles and clips made from metal traded across the southern half of the African continent. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: MIT turns bacteria into living transistors
item.description: MIT researchers have created bacterial “transistors” that can be wired together into living circuits capable of performing calculations and directing chemical signals. One day, these biological computers could coat plant roots or leaves, detecting environmental threats and automatically triggering defenses. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Researchers test far-ultraviolet light to prevent bird flu in poultry
item.description: When a strain of highly pathogenic avian influenza, or HPAI, tore through U.S. poultry farms in early 2025, farmers culled tens of millions of birds, and egg prices soared. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions
item.description: Slow breathing with a prolonged exhale made people more willing to take risks by changing heart activity and increasing the brain’s sensitivity to rewards. The findings suggest that something as simple as controlling your breath can directly influence how you evaluate choices. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Zero‑alcohol drinks are rising in popularity. What do young people think about them?
item.description: Over the past decade, zero-alcohol drinks have gone from a relatively niche product to a staple in supermarket aisles, liquor stores and pubs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Giant Greenland iceberg slams into Joe Island and survives
item.description: A giant iceberg measuring more than 76 square kilometers broke from Greenland’s Petermann Glacier in August 2026, marking the Arctic’s largest glacier calving event since 2020. The berg later slammed into Joe Island but survived without breaking apart, and satellites are now tracking it as it drifts through Nares Strait. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Volunteers fight uphill battle against Indonesian fires
item.description: Twice already this week, Indonesian volunteer firefighter Kristoforus Sinyong worked throughout the night fighting some of the blazes that have consumed swaths of the island of Borneo. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Which of the seven wonders of the ancient world would you most like to have seen in its heyday?
item.description: Which of the seven wonders of the ancient world would you most like to have seen in its heyday? Given it existed and somewhat in the form we imagine the hanging gardens for sure Ver más comentarios Stefan Cizinsky Ver las 2 respuestas Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Dying radio galaxies fade faster than scientists expected
item.description: Astronomers have identified a surprisingly young population of fading radio galaxies whose supermassive black holes have already switched off their powerful jets. The confirmed remnants range from about 8 to 42 million years old, suggesting many may disappear from view much faster than previously recognized. More distant remnants also seem to fade especially quickly, helping explain why they have been so difficult to detect. Fuente: ScienceDaily.
